justification: Originality: the article's central differentiator — a runnable failing unit test (bad-singleton-test) that demonstrates the exact coupling a static-Instance Singleton creates, followed by a constructor-injection rewrite that passes (good-singleton-test) and a citation of Microsoft's own 'don't implement the singleton design pattern' DI guidance — genuinely exceeds the current top results for 'factory pattern c#'. I fetched two prominent existing pages: refactoring.guru's Singleton/C# example mentions unit-test limitations in one throwaway sentence with no demonstration and never discusses DI containers as the resolution; dofactory's Factory Method page doesn't compare any of the four patterns, and has no testability or DI content at all. Neither page does what this article does: show the test failing, then show it passing after a structural change, then explain why. That matches the CONTENT_PLAN.md row 6 angle ('Honest singleton critique with testability demo') precisely, and it is the strongest section of the piece. The Builder section's distinction between GoF's two-role Director-driven Builder and the single-role fluent shape nearly every modern C# 'builder' actually uses (StringBuilder, WebApplicationBuilder, this article's own HttpRequestBuilder) is also a real, non-generic observation that most tutorial-level 'builder pattern c#' content skips by presenting the fluent shape as if it were the GoF pattern unchanged. Sourcing: I fetched all four Microsoft Learn pages that supply direct quotations and checked every one against the live page text. Lazy<T>'s thread-safety quotes ('by default, all public and protected members of the Lazy<T> class are thread safe...' and the ExecutionAndPublication/None table entries) match verbatim. StringBuilder's immutability and chaining quotes match verbatim. The DI overview's 'difficult to unit test' / 'the app should use a mock or stub... which isn't possible with this approach' matches verbatim (the ellipsis correctly elides only the MessageWriter class name, not reordered content). One sourcing issue did surface, listed below: the service-lifetimes quotation splices two sentences with an ellipsis in the reverse of their order in the source. No filler: the piece opens with a specific claim about the GoF taxonomy, not a restated title or 'in this article'; there is no boilerplate conclusion — it ends inside a worked exercise solution. Headings are specific to content ('Simple factory: one method, a switch, no pattern name', 'What a global singleton costs a test suite') and do not repeat the generic Introduction/Conclusion shape. I compared headings against three pillar siblings (composition-over-inheritance.md, strategy-observer-decorator.md, interfaces-vs-abstract-classes.md) and found no template repetition — each article's heading set and rhythm is its own. Front matter is accurate and non-clickbait: the title names exactly what the piece does (compares the four patterns, singles out Singleton for critique) and the description doesn't oversell. No NEEDS_MARKUS markers, no lorem ipsum/placeholder text, no ad code — checked by direct grep. Two concrete defects keep this off a higher score, both listed below: a duplicated exercise-setup paragraph that restates the same scenario twice in slightly different words, which reads as an unremoved draft artifact, and the reordered DI-lifetimes quotation.

issues.location: 'Find the missing guarantee' exercise intro (immediately after the Singleton/Lazy<T> diagram, before the exercise question)
issues.problem: The exercise setup states the same fact twice in consecutive paragraphs: 'This rewrite of `AppConfiguration` drops the `LazyThreadSafetyMode` argument's usual justification — someone reasoned that a lambda with no side effects other than the constructor "can't race":' is immediately followed by a second paragraph, 'This rewrite of `AppConfiguration` replaces `LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication` with `LazyThreadSafetyMode.None` in the `Lazy<T>` field initializer, reasoning that a lambda with no side effects other than the constructor "can't race."' Both paragraphs describe the identical rewrite with the identical quoted justification; nothing in the second sentence adds information the first didn't already give. This reads as a leftover draft fragment (an earlier and a rewritten version of the same sentence both left in), which is exactly the kind of unpolished, redundant text an AdSense reviewer flags as low-effort even though the surrounding article is not.
issues.fixLooksLike: Delete one of the two paragraphs (the second, more precise one, is the better one to keep since it names the actual code change) so the exercise states the scenario once.

issues.location: 'The DI lifetime that replaced it' section: '"don't implement the singleton design pattern and provide code to dispose of the singleton... if the app requires singleton behavior, allow the service container to manage the service's lifetime"[[3]]'
issues.problem: The live Microsoft Learn page (service-lifetimes) has these two sentences in the opposite order: 'If the app requires singleton behavior, allow the service container to manage the service's lifetime. Don't implement the singleton design pattern and provide code to dispose of the singleton.' The article's ellipsis implies material was skipped between two sentences read in their original order; instead the two sentences were reversed. The words themselves are unaltered and the citation is real and accessible, so this is not fabrication, but it misrepresents how the source actually reads, which the editorial brief's citation rule (cite where the claim is made, and make sure that page supports that clause) is meant to guard against.
issues.fixLooksLike: Quote the two sentences in their original order ('if the app requires singleton behavior... don't implement the singleton design pattern...'), or quote only one of the two sentences and paraphrase the other outside the quotation marks.
